subject: Banking
title: Credit Scoring with Machine Learning
description: A 60-second lesson on Credit Scoring with Machine Learning.

hook.text: Traditional credit scores ignore 45 million Americans with thin credit files.

buildup.text: Machine-learning models pull in rent, utility, and cash-flow signals that classic bureaus often miss.

discovery.text: That can surface reliable borrowers who always paid bills but never used credit cards or installment loans.

twist.text: AI credit models risk encoding bias. If training data reflects historical discrimination.

climax.text: AI credit scoring can include millions or exclude them more efficiently. The tool is powerful.

punchline.text: 45 million invisible to FICO. AI can include or exclude them faster.

quiz.question: What is the biggest risk of AI-based credit scoring?
options: Encoding historical discrimination from biased training data

details.summary: Machine learning credit scoring uses thousands of data points beyond traditional credit history, including spending patterns, employment stability, and digital behavior, to assess creditworthiness more accurately for previously unscorable borrowers.
details.whyItMatters: Traditional credit scores exclude billions of people with thin or no credit files. ML models can extend credit to these populations by finding predictive signals in alternative data, potentially transforming financial inclusion worldwide.
takeaways: ML models analyze thousands of variables versus FICO's five major factors
Alternative data like rent and utility payments helps score thin-file borrowers
Bias in training data can lead to discriminatory lending patterns

faq.question: What alternative data do ML credit models use?
faq.answer: Rent payments, utility bills, employment history, education, bank account transaction patterns, and even smartphone usage data. Each data source adds predictive power for borrowers who lack traditional credit history.

faq.question: Is ML credit scoring fair to all applicants?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. Models can discover proxy variables for race, gender, or age that create illegal discrimination. Careful bias testing and regulatory oversight are essential to prevent ML models from perpetuating historical lending discrimination.
